Visarga before c → ś (सेनानीश्चि-); -aḥ before the voiced m → -o (चिक्षुराख्यो).

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (दिगन्तर a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, दिशाम् अन्तरम्)
samasa.literal: that in which the intervals of the directions were kindled
samasa.sense: a battle whose weapons lit up the whole horizon

samasa.vigraha: महिषासुरस्य सेनानीः (सेनानी = सेनां नयति इति, upapada tatpuruṣa with √नी + kvip)

samasa.sense: a mighty asura (महत् becomes महा- as the first member of a karmadhāraya)

morph.note: सेनानी is a root-noun in -ī (from √नी ‘to lead’); its nominative singular keeps the visarga: सेनानीः. Chapter 3 calls Cikṣura सेनानीः again (3.2) and, after his death, महिषस्य चमूपतिः (3.11).
Neuter, to agree with युद्धम् of 2.39: the battle is described before its first fighter is named. आदीपित is the past participle of the causative of आ + √दीप् ‘set ablaze’.

mantras.anvaya: (तत् युद्धं) बहुधा मुक्तैः शस्त्रास्त्रैः आदीपितदिगन्तरम् (आसीत्)। महिषासुरसेनानीः चिक्षुराख्यः महासुरः (2.41: युयुधे)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line qualifies युद्धम् (2.39). The second introduces Cikṣura, the subject of युयुधे at the head of 2.41.
mantras.lit: (a battle) in which the spaces between the quarters were lit up by weapons and missiles discharged in many ways. Mahiṣāsura’s general, the great asura named Cikṣura,
mantras.tr: a battle in which the weapons and missiles they hurled set the whole horizon ablaze. Cikṣura, the mighty asura, Mahiṣāsura’s commander,
mantras.tr_note: The sentence of the second line is completed by युयुधे in 2.41.

comm.t: The battle is first seen as a whole — the horizon lit by weapons — and then its leaders are named one by one, beginning with Cikṣura, Mahiṣa’s commander. He is the first to attack the Goddess in chapter 3 (3.2).

From here to 2.47 the text gives a muster-roll of Mahiṣa’s generals with the size of their forces. Most of them are killed by name in chapter 3: Cikṣura (3.2ff.), Cāmara (3.11–16), Udagra (3.17), Bāṣkala (3.18), Mahāhanu (3.19), Biḍāla (3.20).

samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa (चतुरङ्गबल a karmadhāraya, चतुरङ्गं बलम्; चतुरङ्ग a bahuvrīhi, चत्वारि अङ्गानि यस्य तत्)
samasa.sense: with a full army of elephants, chariots, cavalry and foot

morph.note: Perfect of the ātmanepada root √युध्: reduplication यु- + युध् + -ए. Its subject is Cikṣura (2.40), and it serves Cāmara too.
Instrumental plural of षष् ‘six’: before -भिः the ṣ appears as ḍ (षड्भिः). Six ayutas = sixty thousand.

mantras.anvaya: (चिक्षुराख्यः महासुरः) युयुधे; चामरः च चतुरङ्गबलान्वितः अन्यैः (सह युयुधे)। उदग्राख्यः महासुरः रथानां षड्भिः अयुतैः (2.42: अयुध्यत)।
mantras.anvaya_en: युयुधे closes the sentence of 2.40b and is understood again with Cāmara. The second line names Udagra, whose verb is अयुध्यत at the head of 2.42.
mantras.lit: fought; and Cāmara, with others, accompanied by an army of four divisions. The great asura named Udagra, with six ten-thousands of chariots,
mantras.tr: joined battle; so did Cāmara, with others and an army of all four arms. Udagra, the mighty asura, with sixty thousand chariots,
mantras.tr_note: ‘Sixty thousand’ renders षड्भिः अयुतैः (six ayutas). The second line continues into 2.42.

comm.t: The first three generals: Cikṣura, Cāmara with a full army, and Udagra with sixty thousand chariots. The fourfold army (चतुरङ्ग) is the classical Indian army of elephants, chariots, horse and foot.
The numbers grow as the roll goes on — tens of thousands, then millions, then crores — to show the scale of what one Goddess faces. The point is the disproportion, not the arithmetic.

words.g: √युध् (divādi, 4Ā), laṅ (imperfect), prathama-puruṣa ekavacana, ātmanepada; subject Udagra (2.41), and understood again with Mahāhanu

morph.note: Imperfect of √युध् on the divādi stem युध्य- with augment a-: ‘(he) fought’. Its use beside the perfect युयुधे shows the two tenses alternating freely in narrative.
Nominative of an n-stem (लोमन् ‘hair’) at the end of a bahuvrīhi: -मन् → -मा, as in विश्वकर्मा (2.27).

mantras.anvaya: (उदग्राख्यः महासुरः रथानां षड्भिः अयुतैः) अयुध्यत; महाहनुः च अयुतानां सहस्रेण (अयुध्यत)। असिलोमा महासुरः च पञ्चाशद्भिः नियुतैः (अयुध्यत)।
mantras.anvaya_en: अयुध्यत completes 2.41b and is understood for Mahāhanu and Asiloman. Each general is given with the instrumental of the force that accompanies him.
mantras.lit: fought; and Mahāhanu with a thousand of ten-thousands; and with fifty niyutas the great asura Asiloman,
mantras.tr: fought on, and Mahāhanu with ten million; and the mighty Asiloman with fifty million,
mantras.tr_note: A thousand ayutas is ten million; fifty niyutas is rendered ‘fifty million’, taking a niyuta as a million (see Flags).

comm.t: Udagra fights; Mahāhanu (‘Great-Jaw’) comes with a thousand ayutas, ten million; Asiloman (‘Sword-Hair’) with fifty niyutas. The names describe monstrous bodies.
Mahāhanu is killed by the Goddess’s trident in 3.19. Asiloman is not named again in the Gita Press text of chapter 3.

flags.uncertain: The value of नियुत varies in the lexical tradition (a million in most lists, a hundred thousand in some); fifty niyutas is therefore fifty million or five million.

sandhi.note: Visarga before ṣ may stay (शतैः षड्भिः); after i before the voiced b it appears as r (षड्भिर्बाष्कलो); -aḥ before y becomes -o (बाष्कलो युयुधे).

sandhi.type: vowel sandhi inside a compound (vṛddhi); visarga sandhi
sandhi.note: a + o → au (सहस्रौघ); visarga after ai before a vowel appears as r.

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa; inside it गजवाजिसहस्र is a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (गजवाजिनां सहस्राणि) and गजवाजि an itaretara dvandva (गजाः च वाजिनः च)
samasa.literal: by floods of thousands of elephants and horses
samasa.sense: with wave on wave of elephants and cavalry

morph.note: Past participle of the causative of परि + √वृ: ‘made surrounded, encircled’. It can be read as a name (Parivārita), the subject of अयुध्यत in 2.44, which otherwise has none; or as the plain participle ‘surrounded’, describing Bāṣkala, with 2.44a then repeating his fighting. The name reading is followed here; in 2.45 the same word is plainly the participle.
As in 2.41: six hundreds of ayutas = six million.

mantras.anvaya: बाष्कलः अयुतानां षड्भिः शतैः रणे युयुधे। अनेकैः गजवाजिसहस्रौघैः परिवारितः (2.44: रथानां कोट्या च वृतः तस्मिन् युद्धे अयुध्यत)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is complete. The second introduces परिवारितः, taken as the name of the next general, whose verb is अयुध्यत in 2.44.
mantras.lit: With six hundreds of ten-thousands Bāṣkala fought in the battle. Parivārita, with many hosts of thousands of elephants and horses,
mantras.tr: Bāṣkala fought in the battle with six million. Parivārita, with many thousands of elephants and horses in their hosts,
mantras.tr_note: परिवारितः is rendered as a name (see Morph and Flags); ‘six million’ renders six hundred ayutas.

comm.t: Bāṣkala comes with six hundred ayutas — six million. He is struck down with a bhindipāla in 3.18, where the Gita Press prints the name as वाष्कल (b and v are interchangeable in many manuscripts).

Translators divide the next lines differently. Taking परिवारितः as a name gives each verb of 2.43–45 its own general (Bāṣkala, Parivārita, Biḍāla); taking it as ‘surrounded’ leaves Bāṣkala, or Biḍāla, as the subject of two verbs.

flags.uncertain: परिवारितः may be a proper name (Parivārita) or the participle ‘surrounded’; the name reading is followed because अयुध्यत in 2.44a has no other subject. No general of that name appears among those slain in chapter 3.
